# Model and source

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Bois_1996_benzene"))$reference`
* Description: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Bois_1996_benzene"))$description`
* Article: [Environ Health Perspect 104 Suppl 6:1405-1411 (1996)](https://doi.org/10.1289/ehp.961041405)

Bois and colleagues built a Bayesian (Markov-chain Monte Carlo) population
physiologically based toxicokinetic (PBPK) model for benzene, an environmental
and occupational carcinogen. The body is divided into five flow-limited
compartments -- poorly perfused tissues, well-perfused tissues, fat, bone
marrow and liver -- with instantaneous pulmonary equilibrium between alveolar
air, venous blood and arterial blood. Benzene is metabolized by a
Michaelis-Menten process in the liver and bone marrow; the metabolites, plus an
endogenous baseline formation term, are excreted to urine, where urinary phenol
is a measured output. The model was fit to inhalation-chamber data (blood and
exhaled-air benzene, urinary phenol) from three male volunteers.

The central result is that the **fraction of benzene metabolized is essentially
constant (median ~52%, 90% CI 47-67%) and independent of exposure up to 10 ppm**
-- i.e. metabolism is linear over the studied range -- and that roughly
2-40 mg/day is metabolized in the bone marrow at a continuous 1 ppm exposure.
This vignette reproduces those headline findings from the packaged model.

# Population

The data are from three healthy young white male volunteers (body weights 55,
73 and 90 kg) exposed to benzene in an inhalation chamber for 4 h at 1.7 ppm
(5.2 ug/L) and, one month later, at 10 ppm (30 ug/L). Blood and exhaled-air
benzene and urinary phenol were measured during exposure and over the following
two days (Pekari et al. 1992). The 24 estimated parameters are body-weight
*scaling coefficients* rather than direct physiologic quantities; their
posterior population geometric means (Table 2, column `exp(mu)`) are the model's
typical values and their population heterogeneity (column `exp(Sigma)`,
geometric SDs) is carried as lognormal between-subject variability.

The same information is available programmatically via the model's `population`
metadata (`readModelDb("Bois_1996_benzene")()$population`).

```{r population}
readModelDb("Bois_1996_benzene")()$population[c(
  "species", "n_subjects", "weight_range", "disease_state"
)]
```

# Source trace

Every `ini()` value carries an in-file comment pointing to its source location;
the structural model (five tissue ODEs, pulmonary equilibrium, Michaelis-Menten
metabolism, endogenous phenol formation) is from the Methods and Table 1
scaling functions. Typical values are the posterior population geometric means
of Table 2; between-subject variances are `log(exp(Sigma))^2` from the Table 2
population-SD column.

| Element | Value (typical) | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Ventilation/perfusion ratio `vpr` | 1.7 | Table 2, VPR `exp(mu)` |
| Flow coefficients `scfwp/scfpp/scff/scfbm/scfl` | 0.34 / 0.041 / 0.029 / 0.19 / 1.0 | Table 2 (per unit tissue mass) |
| Volume coefficients `scvwp/scvf/scvbm/scvl` | 0.23 / 0.25 / 0.052 / 0.031 | Table 2 (fractions of LM; fat of WT) |
| Blood/air partition `pba` | 9.65 | Table 2, Pba `exp(mu)` |
| Tissue/blood partitions `pwp/ppp/pf/pbm/pl` | 1.0 / 1.7 / 19 / 7.67 / 1.8 | Table 2 |
| Liver `Vmax` coefficient `scvmaxl` | 5.8 (`Vmax = scvmaxl*LM^0.7`) | Table 2, Vmaxl `exp(mu)` |
| Marrow `Vmax` fraction `scvmaxbm` | 0.16 | Table 2, Vmaxbm `exp(mu)` |
| Liver / marrow first-order rates `rkml/rkmbm` (= Vmax/Km) | 0.60 / 2.8 /min | Table 2, Kml / Kmbm `exp(mu)` |
| Endogenous phenol formation `kf` | 0.014 mg/min | Table 2, Kf `exp(mu)` |
| Metabolite excretion `ke` | 0.0016 /min | Table 2, Ke `exp(mu)` |
| Urine formation `fu` | 0.0025 L/min | Table 2, Fu `exp(mu)` |
| Phenol fraction `fp` | 0.78 | Table 2, fp `exp(mu)` |
| Residual (log-scale SD) blood / air / urine | 0.22 / 0.17 / 0.22 | Results (CV ~24 / 19 / 24%) |

**Units check (per ODE term).** Tissue concentrations `C_i` are mg/L, volumes
`V_i` L, flows `F_i` L/min, so `F_i/V_i*(Cart - C_i/P_i)` is `(L/min)/L * mg/L =
mg/L/min`. The metabolism term `Vmax*C/(Km + C*V)` is `(mg/min)*(mg/L)/mg =
mg/L/min`; multiplying by `V` (L) gives the amount rate mg/min that drives the
metabolite pool `Amet` and the cumulative `AmetL/AmetBM`. The inhaled-amount
rate `Qalv*Cinh` is `(L/min)*(mg/L) = mg/min`. Urinary phenol
`fp*ke*Amet/fu` is `(1/min)*mg / (L/min) = mg/L`. All terms are dimensionally
consistent.

# Simulation setup

Inhalation exposure enters the model as a time-constant air concentration
`CEXP` (mg/L) held while `t < TEXP` (min) -- not as a dose event. The model has
three observation endpoints (venous blood benzene `Cc`, exhaled-air benzene
`Cexh`, urinary phenol `Cphu`), so observation rows carry `dvid = 1` to return
all endpoint columns. Body weight `WT` drives lean body mass and all organ
volumes and flows.

```{r simfun}
bz <- readModelDb("Bois_1996_benzene")

# Typical-value model (between-subject variability zeroed).
bz_tv <- rxode2::zeroRe(bz)

sim_bz <- function(mod, times, wt, cexp, texp) {
  obs <- data.frame(
    id = 1L, time = times, amt = NA_real_, evid = 0L,
    cmt = NA_character_, dvid = 1L, WT = wt
  )
  as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(
    mod, obs,
    params = c(CEXP = cexp, TEXP = texp),
    atol = 1e-12, rtol = 1e-10, maxsteps = 1e6
  ))
}

ppm_to_mgL <- 0.003 / 1 # 1 ppm benzene = 3 ug/L = 0.003 mg/L
```

# Figure replication: chamber time courses (Figures 4 and 5)

Simulated venous-blood and exhaled-air benzene and urinary-phenol time courses
for subject 1 (55 kg) during and after a 4-h exposure, as in Figures 4 and 5 of
Bois 1996. Blood and air benzene rise during the exposure and fall rapidly once
it ends; urinary phenol rises more slowly and returns toward its endogenous
baseline. We show the 10 ppm exposure (Figure 4A/C, Figure 5) and the 1.7 ppm
exposure (Figure 4B/D).

```{r fig-timecourse}
tt <- seq(0, 2880, by = 5) # 48 h, minutes
hi <- sim_bz(bz_tv, tt, wt = 55, cexp = 10 * ppm_to_mgL, texp = 240)
lo <- sim_bz(bz_tv, tt, wt = 55, cexp = 1.7 * ppm_to_mgL, texp = 240)

bz_long <- bind_rows(
  transform(hi, exposure = "10 ppm"),
  transform(lo, exposure = "1.7 ppm")
) |>
  select(time, exposure, Blood = Cc, `Exhaled air` = Cexh, `Urine phenol` = Cphu) |>
  pivot_longer(c("Blood", "Exhaled air", "Urine phenol"),
    names_to = "matrix", values_to = "conc"
  )

ggplot(bz_long, aes(time / 60, conc, colour = exposure)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~matrix, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "Concentration (mg/L)", colour = "Exposure") +
  theme_bw()
```

The peak venous-blood benzene at 10 ppm occurs at the end of exposure (4 h) and
the exhaled-air benzene tracks `Cart/Pba`, one blood/air partition below
arterial blood -- the expected shape for an inhalation exposure.

# Figure replication: exposure-metabolism linearity (Figure 7) and fraction metabolized (Figure 8)

Bois 1996's central finding is that benzene metabolism is **linear** over the
studied range: the amount metabolized scales in direct proportion to exposure,
so the *fraction* metabolized is constant. We reproduce this by equilibrating
the typical individual (73 kg) under continuous exposure for 3 weeks (the paper
verified equilibrium is reached) and computing, over the final day, the amount
metabolized in the bone marrow and the total fraction metabolized.

```{r fig7-linearity}
d3w <- 21 * 24 * 60
grid <- seq(0, d3w, by = 60)
ppm_levels <- c(0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10)

last_day <- function(ppm) {
  s <- sim_bz(bz_tv, grid, wt = 73, cexp = ppm * ppm_to_mgL, texp = 1e12)
  a <- s[nrow(s), ]
  b <- s[s$time == d3w - 1440, ]
  data.frame(
    ppm = ppm,
    bm_mg_day = a$AmetBM - b$AmetBM,
    total_mg_day = (a$AmetL + a$AmetBM) - (b$AmetL + b$AmetBM),
    inhaled_mg_day = a$Ainh - b$Ainh
  )
}

lin <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ppm_levels, last_day))
lin$fraction_pct <- 100 * lin$total_mg_day / lin$inhaled_mg_day
lin

ggplot(lin, aes(ppm, bm_mg_day)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Exposure concentration (ppm)",
    y = "Bone-marrow metabolism (mg/day)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

The log-log slope of bone-marrow metabolism versus exposure is 1 (a straight
line through the origin on linear axes), and the fraction metabolized is
constant across four orders of magnitude of exposure -- exactly the paper's
Figure 7 result. At 1 ppm the bone-marrow amount is within the paper's stated
2-40 mg/day range.

A population cohort (body weight sampled lognormally, geometric mean 73 kg,
geometric SD 1.5, plus the Table 2 between-subject variability) gives the
distribution of the total fraction metabolized at a low exposure, reproducing
Figure 8.

```{r fig8-fraction}
rxode2::rxSetSeed(1996)
nsub <- 150L
set.seed(1996)
wt_cohort <- round(stats::rlnorm(nsub, log(73), log(1.5)), 1)

# Equilibrate each subject under continuous 0.001 ppm; between-subject
# variability is retained (full model, not zeroRe).
coh_obs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nsub), function(i) {
  data.frame(
    id = i, time = c(d3w - 1440, d3w), amt = NA_real_, evid = 0L,
    cmt = NA_character_, dvid = 1L, WT = wt_cohort[i]
  )
}))
coh <- as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(
  bz, coh_obs,
  params = c(CEXP = 0.001 * ppm_to_mgL, TEXP = 1e12),
  atol = 1e-12, rtol = 1e-10, maxsteps = 1e6
))

frac <- coh |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(
    frac_pct = 100 * (diff(AmetL + AmetBM)) / diff(Ainh), .groups = "drop"
  )

quantile(frac$frac_pct, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))

ggplot(frac, aes(frac_pct)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "grey70", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Fraction benzene metabolized per day (%)", y = "Subjects") +
  theme_bw()
```

# Mechanistic validation

Because the model has no administered dose and its endpoints are an inhaled-air
forcing's downstream concentrations, non-compartmental (NCA) analysis is not the
relevant check (the paper reports no NCA parameters). The validations below
instead target the quantitative results the paper does report.

```{r validation-table}
# 1. Fraction metabolized at 1 ppm (typical individual).
f1 <- last_day(1)
frac_typ <- 100 * f1$total_mg_day / f1$inhaled_mg_day

# 2. Linearity: fraction identical across exposure (range over 0.001-10 ppm).
frac_range <- diff(range(lin$fraction_pct))

# 3. Baseline urinary phenol with no exposure (endogenous steady state).
base <- sim_bz(bz_tv, c(0, 600), wt = 73, cexp = 0, texp = 0)
phenol_base <- tail(base$Cphu, 1)

val <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "Fraction metabolized (typical, 1 ppm)",
    "Bone-marrow metabolism at 1 ppm",
    "Fraction metabolized range over 0.001-10 ppm",
    "Population 5th-95th pct fraction metabolized",
    "Baseline urinary phenol (no exposure)"
  ),
  Simulated = c(
    sprintf("%.1f%%", frac_typ),
    sprintf("%.1f mg/day", f1$bm_mg_day),
    sprintf("%.2f pct points", frac_range),
    sprintf("%.0f-%.0f%%", quantile(frac$frac_pct, 0.05), quantile(frac$frac_pct, 0.95)),
    sprintf("%.1f mg/L", phenol_base)
  ),
  Paper = c(
    "~52% (90% CI 47-67%)",
    "2-40 mg/day (geomean ~10)",
    "0 (linear, exposure-independent)",
    "47-67%",
    "~6 (range 1-40)"
  )
)
knitr::kable(val)
```

```{r validation-assertions}
stopifnot(
  # Fraction metabolized sits inside the paper's 90% CI (47-67%).
  frac_typ > 47, frac_typ < 67,
  # Metabolism is linear: the fraction barely moves across 4 orders of
  # magnitude of exposure (the paper's central claim).
  frac_range < 1,
  # Bone-marrow metabolism at 1 ppm is within the stated 2-40 mg/day.
  f1$bm_mg_day > 2, f1$bm_mg_day < 40,
  # Endogenous baseline urinary phenol is within the reported 1-40 mg/L.
  phenol_base > 1, phenol_base < 40,
  # The population central fraction metabolized reproduces the paper's ~52%.
  abs(median(frac$frac_pct) - 52) < 8
)
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Parameters are scaling coefficients, not physiologic values.** The 24
  estimated parameters are body-weight scaling coefficients (Table 1 "scaling
  function" column). The file encodes those scaling functions in `model()`:
  lean body mass `LM = WT*(1 - scvf)`, organ volumes as fractions of `LM` (fat
  as a fraction of `WT`), the poorly perfused volume by difference so organ
  masses plus a 17%-of-LM skeleton sum to `WT`, allometric
  `Vmax,liver = scvmaxl*LM^0.7`, and `Km = Vmax / (Vmax/Km)` using the Table 2
  first-order-rate coefficients.
* **Typical values are posterior population geometric means (Table 2,
  `exp(mu)`).** Between-subject variability is carried as lognormal IIV with
  variance `log(exp(Sigma))^2` from the Table 2 population-SD column. The
  authors note only three young white male subjects were studied, so the
  population spread is narrow and would widen in a broader population.
* **Vmax and Km are weakly identified; their ratio is the meaningful
  quantity.** Because metabolism is linear over the studied range, the paper
  reports that only the `Vmax/Km` scaling coefficients retain meaning (the
  first-order metabolic rate). The file parameterises the liver and bone-marrow
  first-order rates `rkml`, `rkmbm` directly and recovers `Km = Vmax/rate`.
* **Inhalation enters as a concentration forcing.** `CEXP` is the time-constant
  chamber air concentration while `t < TEXP`; there is no dosing compartment.
  The vignette overrides `CEXP`/`TEXP` per scenario. The pulmonary exchange is
  the instantaneous-equilibrium (steady-state lung) form
  `Cart = (Qc*Cven + Qalv*Cinh)/(Qc + Qalv/Pba)`.
* **Phenol submodel lumps one metabolite pool.** The liver and bone-marrow
  metabolite pools are combined into a single pool `Amet` (both are excreted at
  the common rate `Ke`); this is algebraically equivalent to two separate pools
  for the urinary-phenol output. The pool starts at its endogenous steady state
  `Kf/Ke`. With the posterior means the baseline urinary phenol is ~4.4 mg/L,
  slightly below the ~6 mg/L central value the prior was built from but well
  within the reported 1-40 mg/L range.
* **The three subjects' individual parameter columns (Table 2) are not packaged
  separately.** The file ships the population typical values plus IIV; the
  per-subject posteriors are reproducible by fixing `WT` to 55/73/90 kg.
* **No digitised observed data.** The chamber concentration data of Pekari et
  al. were not digitised; the figure-replication chunks show the simulated
  profiles and the validation targets the reported scalar results (fraction
  metabolized, linearity, bone-marrow amount, baseline phenol).
